chunks.heading: This Website
chunks.text: Static site served entirely from AWS — the site is its own case study. Registered domain transferred from GoDaddy to Route 53 (including tearing down a stale DNSSEC chain — DS records deleted at the .dev registry before the nameserver cutover, so resolution never broke). Hosted from S3, fronted by CloudFront with a free ACM certificate. The .dev TLD is HSTS-preloaded, so every connection is HTTPS by force. Keyless CI/CD — OIDC-federated deploys, no stored credentials; every deploy verified byte-for-byte against the commit, behind three drift guards that run before any credential is assumed Security headers at the edge — a path-branched CSP: script-src 'none' on this page, which carries no JavaScript at all, and a separate narrow policy for the chatbot route Self-testing monitoring — alarm → SNS → Lambda → SES, with a monthly heartbeat that shares no failure modes with the path it tests Full write-ups and infrastructure code on GitHub → S3 CloudFront Route 53 ACM DNSSEC Live

chunks.heading: Delivery & Monitoring Pipeline
chunks.text: How this site ships and how it tells on itself when it breaks. Push-to-main deploys assume a least-privilege IAM role through OIDC federation with zero stored AWS keys, then verify the live page byte-matches the commit. GitHub’s undocumented immutable-ID subject claims were diagnosed by decoding the runner’s own JWT. Guards run before credentials — three drift checks (stack manifest, corpus hash, page-asset resolution) block a deploy before any AWS credential is ever assumed Security headers at the edge — CloudFront Functions inject a path-branched CSP: script-src 'none' on the main page, which carries no JavaScript at all, and a separate narrow policy for the chatbot route Mail that actually arrives — a CloudFront 5xx alarm routed through Lambda to SES, signing DKIM as ryangrey.dev via Route 53, so DMARC passes on DKIM alignment where SPF cannot align; built after tracing silent drops to a provider accepting mail and discarding it Monitoring that tests itself — an EventBridge Scheduler heartbeat force-fires that alarm monthly through a path sharing no failure modes with the pipeline it tests, behind an AWS Budgets guardrail Full write-ups and infrastructure code on GitHub → GitHub

chunks.heading: GreyScale — Family Weigh-In on iOS
chunks.text: Private iOS app and serverless backend · no public listing and no public repo, by design A shared spreadsheet had been scoring a four-person family’s weekly weigh-ins since May, and its computed columns had already gone stale. GreyScale replaces it: a SwiftUI app on everyone’s phone over a serverless backend, designed, built and shipped solo. Single-table DynamoDB reached only by Query on the partition key — there is no Scan in the code, and none granted in the IAM policy either. It has since grown a calorie tracker with five ways in: typed, barcode, database search, a photograph of the plate read by Bedrock, and a Nutrition Facts panel read on the phone itself. Nothing derived is ever stored — the table holds a weight and a date; every weekly loss, running total and pass/fail verdict is recomputed from raw weights. A later “rewind to any past week” feature then cost almost nothing to build: showing week 5 is scoring the same rows with the later ones removed, so there is no historical snapshot that can drift out of step Every write is pinned to its author — no endpoint accepts a member id, not the weigh-in, the photo or the profile badges. The row key always derives from the verifi

chunks.heading: Cloud Watchtower — macOS Menu-Bar Monitor
chunks.text: Source on GitHub → A native menu-bar app that answers two questions at a glance: is the site healthy, and what is it costing? CloudFront traffic and error rates, CloudWatch alarm state, and month-to-date spend against the budget. The menu-bar glyph encodes health, so the panel only needs opening when something is actually wrong. No dependencies at all — the AWS SDK for Swift is a 2.3 GB repository, so request signing is written directly instead: AWS SigV4 in about a hundred lines of CryptoKit, covering both the Query/XML and JSON wire protocols Cost is a design constraint — Cost Explorer bills per request, so it never runs on a timer and sits behind a button labelled with its own price; batching every metric into a single call brings the monitor to ~$0.12/month against roughly $8.50 for a poll-everything build — over 60× cheaper Least privilege — it assumes a scoped read-only role on one-hour STS credentials rather than holding the deploy key, and proves which identity it resolved instead of trusting the config Degrades honestly — a failed refresh keeps the last good value with the failure named and its age stated, and the glyph has a third state, because “cannot reach AWS” is not

chunks.heading: AIF Study Engine — Cognito-Gated Exam Prep
chunks.text: Source on GitHub → · private tool at /quiz A spaced-repetition study tool built to pass the AWS AI Practitioner exam, and to get real Cognito experience while doing it. Bedrock writes the questions; the interesting engineering is in what it is not allowed to ask. Scope is a boundary, not a prompt — questions may never cover a lesson not yet completed, so the model is only ever shown in-scope lesson titles AND every question it returns is re-checked against the allowed set, with anything dropped written to the log; a self-test asserts this at all 46 progress markers and gates the deploy Fails closed twice — an API Gateway JWT authorizer rejects unauthenticated calls before any code runs, because generation invokes Bedrock and costs money; the handler then re-verifies the token independently. Sign-in is Cognito Hosted UI with PKCE, no client secret in the browser Designed around the permissions, not against them — the execution role grants no DynamoDB scan and no deletes, so every access path is a Query and retiring a miss is a status flag; the app assumes a scoped read-only role rather than holding a deploy key Spaced repetition that ranks by exam weight — misses return on a 1/3/7-d

chunks.heading: Retrieval-Augmented Chatbot on Amazon Bedrock
chunks.text: Ask the assistant a question → A RAG chatbot grounded in a corpus built from this site and the CV, so it answers from source text instead of hallucinating from general knowledge. Built alongside the AWS AI Practitioner track to understand the retrieval pipeline from the inside — chunking, embedding, and grounding — rather than treating the model as a black box. No vector database — the corpus is embedded with Titan v2 and cosine similarity runs inside the Lambda; a managed vector store at this scale is cost without benefit Answers cite their sources — the model sees only the retrieved chunks and is told to say it doesn't know rather than fill the gap Bounded by design — a public LLM endpoint is an unbounded bill, so per-IP and global caps in DynamoDB fail closed, and the visitor's question is passed to the model as data, never as instructions Amazon Bedrock Nova Lite Titan Embeddings RAG Lambda API Gateway DynamoDB Python Live

chunks.heading: greyBot — Raid Progress & Recaps for Discord
chunks.text: github.com/ryan-grey/greybot Serverless Discord bot that announces a raid guild’s first kill of each boss, and a post-raid recap of how the night went. It reconciles three third-party APIs under a points-budgeted rate limit — one that charges by query complexity rather than by request — and both features share one function and one budget, the recap standing down at a higher reserve so the announcer never loses its headroom to it. Exactly-once delivery — enforced by a DynamoDB conditional write rather than read-then-write: the write that records a kill is the permission to post it, so two overlapping invocations cannot both announce into a live channel. A recap claims its night the same way, keyed on the date the raid started, so one running past midnight is still one night Two raid teams, one log source — no API field separates them, so team identity is derived from who recurs across each tier’s first kills rather than from a roster someone has to keep current. Two signals with a deliberate margin rather than a majority, because people legitimately raid on both teams; when they disagree it posts nothing rather than guess, since the card names individuals. Designed for that case rat
